source_text: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἑξῆς κατηγορῶν τῆς Μω(??)σέως ἱστορίας αἰτιᾶται τοὺς τροπολογοῦντας καὶ ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτήν. ἦν δ᾿ ἂν εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸν γενναιότατον καὶ ἀληθῆ λόγον ἐπιγράψαντα τὸ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίον. τί δήποτε. ὦ οὗτος. θεοὺς μὲν τηλικαύταις περιπίπτοντας συμφοραῖς. ὁποίας ἀναγράφουσιν οἱ σοφοί σου ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ ἐναγέσι μίξεσι χρωμένους καὶ κατὰ τῶν πατέρων στρατευομένους καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα αὐτῶν ἀποτέμνοντας σεμνολογεῖς ἀναγεγράφθαι τὰ τηλικαῦτα τετολμηκέναι καὶ πεποιηκέναι καὶ πεπονθέναι· ὅταν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς μὴ περὶ θεοῦ τοιαῦτα λέγῃ ἀλλὰ μηδ᾿ ἀγγέλων ἁγίων περὶ δὲ ἀνθρώπων πολλῷ ἐλάττονα (οὐδεὶς γὰρ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ἐτόλμησεν ὅσα Κρόνος κατὰ τοῦ Οὐρανοῦ οὐδ᾿ ὅσα Ζεὺς κατὰ τοῦ πατρὸς, οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θυγατρὶ ὁ „πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε“ συνελήλυθεν), πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ; δοκεῖ δὲ μοι καὶ παραπλήσιόν τι Κέλσος ποιεῖν τῷ Πλατωνικῷ Θρασυμάχῳ, μὴ ἐπιτρέποντι ὡς βούλεται ἀποκρίνασθαι περὶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης Σωκράτει ἀλλὰ λέγοντι· ὅρα μὴ τὸ συμφέρον εἴπῃς εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον μηδὲ τὸ δέον μηδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν παραπλησίων. καὶ γὰρ οὗτος κατηγορήσας, ὡς οἴεται. τῶν παρὰ Μωϋσεῖ ἱστοριῶν καὶ μεμψάμενος τοῖς ἀλληγοροῦσι μετὰ τοῦ καὶ ἔπαινόν τινα περὶ αὐτῶν λέγειν, ὅτι εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι. οἱονεὶ κωλύεται κατηγορήσας, ὡς βούλεται, ἀπολογεῖσθαι τοὺς δυναμένους. ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα.
pass_a_gloss: But in the following, accusing the history of Moses, he blames those who interpret it figuratively and allegorize it. It would have been fitting to say to the most noble and true word that has written his own book: what then, oh man? You consider the gods, who have fallen into such great calamities, as the wise poets and philosophers of yours have written, and who have engaged in shameful mixings and have made war against their fathers and have cut off their private parts, to be written about with dignity, the things they have dared and done and suffered; but when Moses does not speak such things about God, nor even about holy angels, but about men, and much lesser things (for no one among them dared as much as Cronus against Uranus, nor as much as Zeus against his father, nor that the 'father of men and gods' had intercourse with his own daughter), do you think you deceive those who have been legislated by him? It seems to me that Celsus does something similar to the Platonic Thrasymachus, who does not allow Socrates to answer as he wishes about justice, but says: see that you do not say that the advantageous is the just, nor the necessary, nor anything else of the like. And this man, having accused, as he thinks, the histories according to Moses, and having found fault with those who allegorize, even praises some for speaking about them, that they are more gentle. As if, having accused as he wishes, he hinders those who are able to defend from defending. As is natural for things to be.

pass_b_english: In what follows, he accuses the history of Moses and blames those who interpret it figuratively and allegorize it. It would have been fitting to say to the most noble and true Word who has written his own book: "What then, man? You regard it as worthy to be recorded with dignity that the gods fell into such great calamities as your wise poets and philosophers have written about, engaged in shameful unions, made war against their fathers, and cut off their private parts—these things they dared, did, and suffered. But when Moses does not speak such things about God, nor even about holy angels, but about human beings and far lesser matters (for no one among them dared what Cronus did against Uranus, nor what Zeus did against his father, nor that the 'father of men and gods' had intercourse with his own daughter), do you think you deceive those who have been legislated by him?" (Genesis 1-3; Exodus 20:12).

It seems to me that Celsus does something similar to the Platonic Thrasymachus, who does not allow Socrates to answer as he wishes about justice, but instead says: "See to it that you do not say the advantageous is the just, nor the necessary, nor anything else of the kind." For this man, having accused, as he thinks, the histories according to Moses, and having found fault with those who allegorize them, even offers some praise for them, saying that they are more moderate. It is as if, having accused as he wishes, he prevents those who are able from making a defense, as is natural for things to be.

review.notes: The translation in Pass B includes added scripture citations that are not present in the Greek source and are contextually incorrect: '(Genesis 1-3; Exodus 20:12)'. The Greek text contains no biblical citations in this paragraph, and the content (discussing Greek mythological crimes of the gods) does not allude to Genesis 1-3 or Exodus 20:12. Per the rules, added identifications are required, but they must not be false. Furthermore, the notes admit the biblical references are 'not clear' and 'alluded to' despite being explicitly inserted into the translation text in Pass B.
